key_terms.meaning: Operations that take an image in and give an image out, such as denoising, enhancement or compression.
Building measurements, labels or decisions from an image, such as counting defects or reading a number plate.
Capturing scene energy with a sensor and turning it into an array of numbers.
Splitting an image into regions or objects, for example separating heart from lung in a chest X-ray.
Undoing known degradations such as blur or sensor noise, using a model of how the image was spoiled.
The eye's ability to re-scale its response over a huge range of light levels, from starlight to sunlight.
ΔI / I, the smallest brightness change ΔI a viewer can notice on a background of intensity I; smaller means finer discrimination.
Two photoreceptor types in the retina: rods work in dim light and sense brightness only, cones work in bright light and sense colour.
The ordered range of radiation by wavelength, from gamma rays through visible light (about 400 nm to 700 nm) to radio waves.
A solid-state array that converts light falling on each small cell into an electric charge, which is read out as a pixel value.
The mapping x = f·X/Z, y = f·Y/Z, giving image coordinates (x, y) of a scene point (X, Y, Z) seen through a lens of focal length f.
The model of how much light a pixel receives, depending on source, surface albedo, surface normal and viewing angle.
Choosing a finite grid of points at which the continuous scene is measured; spacing sets the spatial detail captured.
Rounding each sampled value to one of a fixed set of levels; with n bits there are 2ⁿ levels.
The smallest detail an image can show, set by pixel spacing; often quoted as dots per inch or pixel count.
For pixel p at (x, y), the 4-neighbours are the pixels one step up, down, left or right; the 8-neighbours add the four diagonal pixels.
Two pixels are connected if they are neighbours and their values satisfy a stated similarity rule, for example equal or inside a set S.
For points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): D₄ = |x₁−x₂| + |y₁−y₂| and D₈ = max(|x₁−x₂|, |y₁−y₂|); D₄ counts axis moves, D₈ allows diagonal moves.
Pixel-by-pixel addition, subtraction, multiplication or division of two images, or of an image and a constant.
An operation that moves coordinates rather than values: translation, rotation, scaling, and the interpolation needed to fill the new grid.
A model that gives hue (colour angle), saturation (purity) and intensity (brightness) separately, useful when lighting changes.

takeaways: Image processing keeps the output as an image; computer vision turns the image into a number, a label or a decision, and practical systems need both.
Every imaging system is a chain of blocks: acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, restoration, colour, compression, segmentation, representation, recognition, display.
The eye is a non-linear, locally adapting sensor, so a display with 256 levels per channel already matches what a person can distinguish in one view.
An image becomes numbers only after a sensor converts scene energy to charge, and after sampling picks the grid and quantization picks the levels.
Spatial resolution controls fine detail and intensity resolution controls smooth shading; the two trade against each other for a fixed number of bits.
Neighbours, connectivity and distance measures are the definitions that let us talk about blobs, boundaries and objects instead of isolated pixels.
Arithmetic, logical and geometric operations are the three basic ways to combine or reshape images before any higher-level analysis.
RGB is good for capture and display; HSI is good for algorithms that must ignore brightness, such as colour-based segmentation.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for the block diagram of an image processing system with the function of each step, or for a worked example on sampling, quantization, connectivity and distance measures.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a digital image processing system and explain the function of each fundamental step from acquisition to display.
outline: Acquisition converts scene energy into a digital array
Preprocessing removes obvious defects such as sensor noise
Enhancement makes the image more suitable for a stated task
Restoration uses a degradation model to undo blur or noise
Colour processing handles colour spaces and colour-based operations
Compression reduces storage and transmission cost
Segmentation partitions the image into regions of interest
Representation and description turn regions into features
Recognition assigns labels or decisions
Each step feeds the next; feedback loops exist in practice

bank.q: Describe the structure of the human eye and explain brightness adaptation, the Weber ratio and the Mach band effect.
outline: Cornea and lens focus light on the retina
Retina has rods (dim light, no colour) and cones (bright light, colour)
Rods and cones are not uniformly distributed; the fovea is cone-rich
Brightness adaptation lets the eye cover a very wide range of light levels
Weber ratio ΔI/I measures the smallest detectable brightness change
Discrimination is finer on a plain background than on a textured one
Mach bands are an example of lateral inhibition producing an illusion of extra edge contrast
These limits explain why 8-bit displays look smooth and why pseudo-contouring appears at low bit depth

bank.q: Define sampling and quantization. Explain spatial resolution and intensity resolution, and how each affects the appearance of an image.
outline: Sampling: measuring the continuous scene on a discrete grid
Quantization: rounding each sample to one of 2ⁿ levels
Spatial resolution: pixel spacing or pixel density, controls fine detail
Intensity resolution: number of grey levels per pixel
Too few samples give jagged, blocky shapes (aliasing)
Too few levels give false contours and visible banding
Both are needed to represent a scene; trade bits between them for a fixed budget

bank.q: Define 4-neighbours, 8-neighbours, m-connectivity and the distance measures D₄, D₈ and Dₑ between pixels.
outline: 4-neighbours of p: (x±1, y) and (x, y±1)
8-neighbours add the four diagonal pixels
Adjacency as a special case of connectivity: same value (or inside set S) and neighbours
m-connectivity removes ambiguous diagonal joins present in 8-connectivity
D₄ = |x₁−x₂| + |y₁−y₂|, city-block
D₈ = max(|x₁−x₂|, |y₁−y₂|), chessboard
Euclidean distance Dₑ = √((x₁−x₂)² + (y₁−y₂)²)
Worked example on a small grid

bank.q: A 1024 × 1024 grey image uses 8 bits per pixel. Compute its storage in bytes. Find the storage if it is subsampled to 512 × 512 and quantized to 4 bits, and state what is lost.
outline: Original: 1024 × 1024 × 1 byte = 1 048 576 bytes, about 1 MB
New: 512 × 512 × 0.5 bytes = 131 072 bytes, about 128 KB
One-eighth of the original storage
Loss of spatial detail (half the linear resolution)
Loss of intensity detail (16 levels instead of 256)
Comment on banding and jagged edges

bank.q: Given pixels p at (2, 3) and q at (6, 5) in a grid, compute D₄, D₈ and the Euclidean distance, and list the 4-neighbours of p.
outline: State that D₈ ≤ Dₑ ≤ D₄ always holds
Brief note on which distance suits path length and which suits blob size

bank.q: A scene is captured 25 times with random sensor noise. Explain how averaging the frames changes the noise, compute the improvement, and state two limits of the method.
outline: Averaging N frames reduces random noise standard deviation by √N
For N = 25 the noise falls by a factor of 5
Algorithm: sum the frames, divide by N; use integer arithmetic with a wider type
Limit 1: moving objects smear
Limit 2: needs a static camera and static scene
Limit 3: does not remove fixed-pattern or systematic error
Connection to image addition and division operations

bank.q: A pinhole camera of focal length 50 mm views a 1.8 m tall person at 5 m. Compute the image height and explain what changes if the focal length is doubled.
outline: Use h_image / h_object = f / Z
Doubling f doubles the image size to 36 mm
Field of view narrows as f grows
Assumptions: thin lens, small angles, object parallel to image plane

bank.q: Convert the RGB triple (255, 0, 0) and (128, 128, 128) to HSI, and explain why HSI is preferred for segmenting a red object under changing light.
outline: Intensity I = (R + G + B) / 3
Saturation S = 1 − 3·min(R,G,B) / (R+G+B)
Pure red: H = 0°, S = 1, I = 1/3 in normalised units
Grey (128,128,128): S = 0, hue undefined, I = 128/255
Hue is roughly constant under a brightness change, so thresholding on H is more stable than on R
Saturation guards against picking up washed-out pixels

bank.q: Distinguish image processing, computer vision and computer graphics, giving one Indian application of each, and show where the three meet in a real pipeline.
outline: Image processing: image in, image out
Computer vision: image in, decision or measurement out
Computer graphics: model in, image out
Applications: preprocessing satellite data; reading vehicle number plates; rendering a cricket match replay
Meeting point: a rendered scene is captured, processed, then recognised; vision models are also used to check rendered output
Shared tools: filtering, geometry, colour models

bank.q: A 12-bit medical image is shown on an 8-bit display with simple linear scaling. Analyse what the viewer loses and propose two better display mappings.
outline: Only 256 of 4096 levels can be shown, so most fine differences map to the same display value
The eye's Weber ratio means it cannot see all 4096 levels at once anyway, so windowing is legitimate
Simple scaling wastes levels on empty ranges such as air background
Proposal 1: window and level — map a chosen intensity band to full range
Proposal 2: gamma or logarithmic mapping to spread dark values
Proposal 3: histogram equalisation or CLAHE for local contrast
Note pseudo-contouring risk when the band is too narrow
Mention that true diagnosis needs the original data, not the display

bank.q: Compare arithmetic, logical and geometric operations on images. Give one practical use of each and one numerical hazard of each.
outline: Arithmetic works on values: add, subtract, multiply, divide
Use: frame averaging for noise, subtraction for motion detection
Hazard: overflow and underflow outside 0–255; clip or rescale
Logical works on bits or masks: AND, OR, NOT, XOR
Use: masking a region of interest, bit-plane slicing
Hazard: wrong mask polarity silently removes the region you wanted
Geometric works on coordinates: translate, rotate, scale
Use: aligning two scans, correcting lens distortion
Hazard: interpolation choice changes values; aliasing when shrinking
Conclusion: pick by what is being changed — value, bit or coordinate

bank.q: Design a complete pipeline, from sensor to decision, for automatically reading number plates at a toll plaza. Name the step of the image processing chain used at each stage.
outline: Acquisition: camera and illumination, fixed exposure, synchronised trigger
Preprocessing: denoise, correct lens distortion, convert to grey
Enhancement: contrast stretch or histogram equalisation for night frames
Segmentation: locate the plate region, using edges and connected components
Morphology and connectivity rules to join plate characters
Representation and description: character bounding boxes, size and aspect filters
Recognition: template or classifier per character; confidence threshold
Compression: store only kept frames to save bandwidth
Feedback: log failures and retune thresholds
Mention resolution needed: character height in pixels must be large enough for the classifier

bank.q: Justify the statement that sampling and quantization are the two independent choices that fix an image's information content. Use a fixed budget in bits to argue the trade-off.
outline: An image of M × N pixels with n bits per pixel needs M·N·n bits
Sampling fixes M and N; quantization fixes n
For a fixed total, more pixels means fewer levels and vice versa
Human vision is more sensitive to intensity banding in smooth regions than to small detail loss in textured regions
Aliasing appears before quantisation banding when sampling is reduced too far, for edges and fine texture
Practical rule: fix the sample spacing from the smallest object you must see, then spend remaining bits on intensity
Give a numeric example at a fixed 64 Kbit budget

glossary.def: A finite 2-D array f(x, y) whose entries are brightness values at sampled grid points.
One element of a digital image, identified by its row and column index and holding one or more values.
The brightness value stored at a pixel, usually an integer from 0 to 2ⁿ−1 for n bits.
Early operations that clean an image, such as noise removal or correcting illumination, before the main task.
Processing that makes an image more useful for a viewer or a later algorithm, without a physical model of degradation.
Encoding an image with fewer bits, either losslessly or by discarding detail the viewer will not notice.
Assigning a label or class to a segmented region or to the whole image.
The small central patch of the retina packed with cones, giving the sharpest vision.
Neighbouring retinal cells suppress each other, which sharpens edges and produces effects such as Mach bands.
The fraction of light a surface reflects; a white wall has high albedo and a black cloth low albedo.
A curved refracting element that focuses scene light onto the sensor plane.
A colour filter array over a sensor with more green than red or blue cells, demosaiced later to give full colour.
False low-frequency patterns created when a scene is sampled too coarsely for its detail, seen as jagged edges or moiré.
One of the discrete intensity values available at a given bit depth; 8 bits give 256 grey levels.
A count of how many pixels take each intensity value, used to judge contrast and to drive equalisation.
The relation between two pixels that are neighbours and whose values satisfy a similarity rule.
The set of pixels in a region that have at least one neighbour outside the region.
Estimating pixel values at new coordinates, by nearest-neighbour, bilinear or bicubic rules.
The 2-D binary image formed by taking one bit position from every pixel, useful for showing subtle texture.
A colour system in which lights add, so red plus green plus blue at full strength gives white.
The attribute of colour that we name as red, green or blue, measured as an angle on the colour circle.
How pure a colour is, from 0 for grey to 1 for a fully saturated hue.
A power-law mapping applied so that stored values match how a display and the eye respond.
The ratio between the brightest and darkest values a sensor, display or scene can handle.
